doc.title: Jonathan Scales interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 23, 2025

title: How many pans: the steel orchestra
summary: He explains the pan families, from tenor to double seconds, guitar and cello pans, and the six bass barrels.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: I do. That’s some heady stuff. I appreciate you sharing it with me. Let’s talk about the mechanics of the instrument a bit. Like most people, I don’t quite understand the pans all that much. I had an interesting experience many years ago when I was part time teaching in the Utica, New York public school system and there was an elementary school band that had a pan orchestra. And I got the job of, you know, “Teach some kids this thing.” I had no idea what I was doing. But I remember going around looking at the pans and saying, “Okay this one has these notes and this one has these notes.” So my question to you is how many pans do you really need to have all the notes at your disposal? And do you play custom-made pans?

Okay so in the world of – in the steel pan world it’s kind of like an orchestra. How in an orchestra how you have violin, viola, cello, bass. You know? Each of those groupings of steel pan is a different set-up. Each of those set-ups include all of the notes chromatically on their own. So like if you play the top voice, which ironically is called the tenor pan – it’s not the tenor voice, long story. We’ll talk about that later. The top voice, which is like the soprano voice in the steel orchestra, is called the tenor pan. You’re going to have all of your notes in one pan chromatically, how ever many octaves that your pan is, right? That’s like the violin of the steel orchestra. The instrument I play is called – in the steel pan world it’s called the “double seconds.” That’s just what they’re called. The double seconds is like more of an alto voice. So in order to get all those notes I need two pans. And so all of my notes chromatically are within those two instruments. Right? Now if you go a step below that there is a pan called the “Guitar Pan” and the “Cello Pan” and those pans, they do a lot more like the lower comping and they’re literally like the cellos or like a guitar that’s strumming. That’s why they’re called that. Right? Because it’s their role in the steel orchestra. They have three pans with longer skirts that have like lower sounds, and they take that role. And between those three drums they have all the commanding notes. Right? Now you go down all the way to the bottom. The bottom is, you have six full sized oil barrels with only three notes each. And you need six of those

to chromatically have all the notes for the bass. So you really have the full range of the orchestra and each instrument embodies like a whole spectrum of tones. Just like you have a violin, viola, cello and bass.
